To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
integrated water quality modelling is a complex process that requires the adoption of a systematic and iterative approach to model development and evaluation.

the future of integrated water quality model development is closely related to the development of process‐oriented field studies that provide the basis for the improvement of the model structure and the parameterization of model processes.

(i) integrated water quality models should account for the spatial heterogeneity of the biogeochemical conditions in the catchment and receiving waterbody, (ii) process‐oriented field studies are needed for better articulating model structure, and (iii) the Bayesian inference is an efficient tool for rigorous assessment of integrated water quality model credibility and predictive capacity.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a new generation of coupled landscape‐waterbody models that can be effectively used to assess and predict the impact of land‐use and climate changes on water quality and aquatic biogeochemical cycles.

improving the understanding of the biogeochemical cycling of nutrients at the watershed‐stream continuum and with developing integrated water quality models capable of predicting the effects of land use and climate change on receiving water quality.

the development of novel modelling approaches and techniques to better understand and quantify the role of catchment and in-stream biogeochemical dynamics for water quality and nutrient fate in streams and rivers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
integrated water quality modelling is a challenging task, and that there is a need to improve our knowledge and understanding of the underlying processes.
the current state of knowledge is insufficient to develop reliable and predictive integrated water quality models.
the current integrated water quality models have reached a level of sophistication that enables their use for a number of practical purposes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we need to develop integrated water quality models which are more realistic, more flexible, more efficient, more robust, and more reliable.

we are still at the beginning of our journey to understand the complex interactions between catchment and receiving waterbody biogeochemistry and the processes that control the transport and transformation of water quality constituents.

the future development of integrated water models should focus on (1) the improvement of process descriptions and parameter estimation, (2) the development of novel techniques for model calibration and uncertainty analysis, and (3) the development of integrated modelling frameworks for water quality management and decision support.
The main takeaway from our work is that
integrated water quality modelling will remain a challenging endeavour in the foreseeable future.

the development of integrated water models that are able to effectively account for the complexity of the coupled watershed‐in‐stream processes and the associated uncertainties requires the use of novel modelling approaches that are able to accommodate both the process and data complexities.
the future success of integrated water quality modeling depends on the development of a more comprehensive understanding of landscape and in-stream biogeochemical process dynamics.
